about: Documented reference procedures shown next to an episode, per fault class. Written in our own words as a checklist; each entry cites the public document it follows. These are REFERENCE material, not instructions for a specific machine: always follow the machine manufacturer's manual and site safety rules (lock-out/tag-out). Sites add their own SOPs in knowledge/site_procedures.json (same format, source.kind = 'site SOP').

procedures.title: Rolling bearing defect: confirm, replace, find the cause
confirm_first: The defect-frequency hint (BPFO outer race, BPFI inner race, BSF ball) repeats over several windows and grows or stays, rather than a one-off spike.
Check lubrication state and temperature; lubrication problems can produce similar high-frequency signs.
steps: Plan the replacement; do not run to destruction if the severity zone is C or D.
Lock out the machine; remove the bearing with the correct puller or induction heater (no hammer blows through the rolling elements).
Inspect the removed bearing and classify the damage by failure mode (fatigue, wear, corrosion, electrical erosion, plastic deformation, fracture) - this is what tells the root cause.
Check shaft and housing seats for wear, fretting or out-of-round before fitting the new bearing.
Mount the new bearing with the correct method and fit; lubricate with the specified grease/oil and quantity.
Record the found damage mode as the root-cause claim (it becomes fleet evidence).
procedures.system_verifies: After the action is recorded, the device counts N consecutive windows back inside this machine's healthy radius (symptom resolved), or reports that the symptom persists.

sources.title: Bearing damage and failure analysis (publication 14219, based on ISO 15243 failure modes)

procedures.title: Imbalance (dominant 1x): clean, inspect, then balance
confirm_first: The 1x (once per revolution) peak dominates and is steady; 2x and higher harmonics are small.
Rule out simple causes first: dirt build-up or a damaged/missing blade or part on the rotor.
steps: Lock out; clean the rotor/blades and inspect for damage, missing balance weights or loose parts.
If still unbalanced: single-plane field balancing (fans, discs, short rotors) - measure the as-found 1x amplitude and phase (reference run).
Attach a known trial weight at a marked angle, run again and measure the new 1x amplitude and phase (trial run).
Compute the correction mass and angle from the change the trial weight caused (the influence), remove the trial weight, fit the correction and re-measure.
Repeat a trim run if the residual 1x is still high.
procedures.system_verifies: The device verifies that windows return to the healthy radius; on a phone-grade sensor this confirms the 1x symptom dropped, not the balance grade.

sources.title: Balancing Rigid Rotors in the Field

procedures.title: Misalignment (strong 2x): soft foot first, then align
confirm_first: 2x is large relative to 1x (and often axial vibration is high); coupling temperature or wear may be visible.
On low sampling rates (e.g. a 60 Hz phone) 2x may be above the Nyquist limit: the system then says misalignment is NOT assessable.
steps: Pre-alignment checks: machine locked out, feet and base clean, bolts, pipe strain, coupling condition.
Check and correct soft foot (a foot not sitting flat distorts the frame and can itself show up as vibration).
Rough-align, then measure alignment (laser system or dial indicators) and correct vertical and horizontal offset and angularity to tolerance.
Re-check soft foot, tighten in the correct sequence, and record the final alignment.
procedures.system_verifies: Windows return to the healthy radius over N windows after the action.

sources.title: Soft Foot: The First Step to Precision Alignment

procedures.title: Looseness (many harmonics / 0.5x): check the mounting
confirm_first: Many harmonics of 1x and/or half-order (0.5x) components; the pattern may change with direction and load.
Soft foot can look like looseness: check it together.
steps: Lock out; check hold-down bolts, base and frame for cracks, and bearing housing fits.
Check for soft foot and correct it; tighten fasteners in sequence to the manufacturer's torque.
Check for rotating looseness (worn bearing fit on the shaft or in the housing) if the structure is sound.
procedures.system_verifies: Windows return to the healthy radius over N windows after the action.

sources.title: Soft Foot: The First Step to Precision Alignment (soft foot seen as looseness)

procedures.title: Bearing running hot or wearing: check lubrication first
confirm_first: Is the housing hotter than usual for this machine and load? Temperature rises also come from overload or misalignment.
Was the bearing greased recently? Too much grease (no running-in) heats a bearing as surely as too little.
steps: Lock out; check the grease type and quantity against the machine documentation (wrong or mixed greases are a common cause).
Relubricate with the specified grease and quantity for this bearing; the bearing maker gives the fill quantity and the relubrication interval for its size, speed and temperature.
After greasing, run in at low speed if possible so excess grease can be displaced, then watch the temperature settle.
Remember the temperature rule of thumb from the source: grease life roughly halves for every 15 C above 70 C, so a hot bearing needs shorter relubrication intervals.
If temperature or vibration stays high, inspect for misalignment, overload or bearing damage (see the other procedures).
procedures.system_verifies: The device verifies that vibration windows return to the healthy radius over N windows after the action.
